Five Apple Watch models can measure your blood pressure, potentially alerting you to possible high blood pressure issues. However, these devices will not provide actual blood pressure readings.

Some smart rings and other fitness devices also have this function, but require periodic calibration with a traditional upper-arm blood pressure monitor. The upcoming Signal Ring claims to provide complete blood pressure measurements without any calibration, and says clinical trials involving thousands of people support this claim...

"Silent Killer"

Abnormally high blood pressure (hypertension) and abnormally low blood pressure (hypotension) can both pose significant health risks.

Of the two, high blood pressure is the more dangerous, often called the "silent killer" because it can cause serious and irreversible damage to the arteries, heart, and brain without any obvious symptoms. In many cases, it is only discovered after triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Elderly people in particular should monitor their blood pressure regularly, and home upper-arm blood pressure monitors are widely available for convenient self-measurement. However, it would be ideal if the fitness device you're wearing could monitor blood pressure fully automatically.

Apple Watch blood pressure feature

After the launch of watchOS 26, five Apple Watch models will be able to measure blood pressure:

  • Apple Watch Series 11
  • Apple Watch Series 10
  • Apple Watch Series 9
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3
  • Apple Watch Ultra 2

However, these devices will not provide any readings, only alerting you when potential signs of high blood pressure are detected. Other devices such as the Oura Ring work in a similar way.

Some fitness devices can indeed provide actual blood pressure readings, but require periodic calibration with readings from a blood pressure monitor.

Signal Ring

Startup company Vital Signals says it has developed a smart ring called the Signal Ring that can measure blood pressure without any calibration, with accuracy comparable to traditional upper-arm blood pressure monitors.

According to Bloomberg, CEO Tom Moss said he almost died from undiagnosed high blood pressure, which is exactly why he founded the company.

The ring will begin pre-orders later today, ship in October, and is priced at $399 with no subscription required. The accompanying app (see image above) can display real-time blood pressure readings and long-term blood pressure trends.

It is worth noting that the Oura Ring has not yet received approval from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), but clinical trials have shown that the device can provide accurate blood pressure readings for thousands of participants.

Interestingly, Moss has no intention of selling this ring to everyone. He said these professional features are most suitable for elderly people and those assessed by doctors as being at risk of high blood pressure, implying that the Signal Ring's performance in other areas (such as sleep tracking) is relatively mediocre.
